beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Bear. Ask an agent to convert a twenty-four chapter textbook into something new, and the tempting move is to just start rewriting chapter one. AI1 CLI refuses. Before a single new chapter drafts, the book has to survive four gates — and the last one, by the system's own constitution, the agent is not allowed to sign. Let's see why.

beats.narration_text: Four gates, in order. Inventory: read every chapter of the old book and say, honestly, what it teaches. Research: commission real evidence instead of trusting anyone's memory. Blueprint: draft the new book's plan from that evidence. And sign-off — GATE zero. The system's own rule, verbatim: 'the agent prepares, the human signs.' Skip a gate, and the drift starts before word one.

beats.narration_text: Inventory sounds administrative. It isn't. It's an archivist's job: open the actual chapter, not its title, and say — in one honest line — what it teaches. Twenty-four chapters, each read this way, no skimming. That discipline is the cheapest gate to fake, and the first one this system refuses to.

shot.prompt: A real archival photograph of a library card catalog, archive reading room, or ledger book close-up — hands or eyes actually engaging with the record, not a staged stock photo. Public-domain (Smithsonian Open Access preferred; Wikimedia Commons / Library of Congress as alternates).

beats.narration_text: The agent's first inventory line for chapter seventeen: 'a longer, more in-depth version of the profile.' Read the actual chapter, though, and it's a qualitative-research chapter — methods, ethics — a different genre wearing the old one's name. The book's own rule: the inventory is a claim, and you just checked it. One wrong row out of twenty-four — about the hit rate you should expect.

beats.act: Act 3 — the prompt that got rejected
beats.narration_text: The research prompt failed the same way, once. The agent's first draft was elaborate — nested taxonomies, a grading rubric, three-tier source scoring. Impressive, and useless: the author's honest verdict was 'I don't understand that prompt at all.' A prompt the human can't read is a prompt the human can't judge. The replacement — four plain questions a stranger could answer.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Four gates run in order before any new chapter drafts: inventory, research, blueprint, sign-off — GATE zero. The constitution's rule, verbatim: 'the agent prepares, the human signs' — sign-off is the one step the agent cannot perform. The inventory step caught its own error live: one wrong row out of twenty-four, found by actually reading. And an unreadable prompt got rejected on the spot and replaced with four questions a stranger could answer.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — here's the prompt, read it with me. 'Before I let you draft anything new from a source document I already trust, make me an inventory table of what it actually teaches, chapter by chapter — and tell me which single line you're least sure about, so I check that one first.' That last clause is the whole method: the agent flags its own weakest guess, and you check that one first. Run it. Liam, in for Bear.
